title: The Carroll A. Deering: Where Did the Ghost Ship's 11 Men Go?
subject: deering
description:
Mutiny, pirates or something else: what do you think happened to the crew? 👇

In January 1921, a five-masted schooner ran aground on Diamond Shoals off Cape Hatteras with her sails set, her lights burning and food in the galley. Her eleven men were gone. This case file follows the mate's threat in Barbados, the last sighting at the Cape Lookout lightship, the faked bottle message and the federal investigation that never closed the case.

Sources: U.S. National Archives, Herbert Hoover Presidential Library ("The Wreck of the Carroll A. Deering"); U.S. Coast Guard ("Ghostship Carroll A. Deering"); National Park Service, Cape Hatteras National Seashore; North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources; Wikipedia, "Carroll A. Deering" and its references.

scenes.text: At first light on the 31st of January, 1921, a Coast Guard lookout at Cape Hatteras saw a five-masted schooner sitting on the outer edge of Diamond Shoals. Every sail was set.
She flew no distress flag, and nobody waved from the rail. The surf was so heavy that for four days no boat could reach her.
When a salvage captain climbed aboard, he found her running lights still burning. In the galley, food had been prepared for a meal that was never eaten.
Both boats were gone, and so were the log, the chronometer and every man of the crew. The only living things aboard were three half-starved cats.
The ship was the Carroll A. Deering, less than two years old. Five government departments would spend more than a year trying to find out where her eleven men went.
She was launched in April 1919 at the G. G. Deering yard in Bath, Maine, and named for the owner's son. At 255 feet, she was one of the last big wooden cargo schooners on the coast.
In August 1920 she loaded coal at Newport News, Virginia, bound for Rio de Janeiro. Her master was Captain William Merritt, with his son Sewall as first mate.
Days into the voyage, Merritt fell seriously ill. The schooner put into Lewes, Delaware, and father and son went ashore. The company needed a new captain quickly.
They found Willis B. Wormell, a Maine captain who had practically retired. In the Coast Guard's own account of the case, he appears simply as Old Man Wormell.
With him came a new first mate, Charles McLellan. The rest of the crew was a mix: an American engineer named Herbert Bates, a Finnish boatswain, a steward, and six Danish sailors.
On the 8th of September they sailed again. Wormell delivered the coal in Rio without trouble, but he told a friend there that he had little respect for most of his crew.
The one man he said he trusted was the engineer, Bates. On the 2nd of December the Deering left Brazil, running empty, and turned north toward Barbados.
In Barbados, the first mate went ashore and drank. He complained to another captain that Wormell would not let him discipline the men and that he had to do the navigating himself.
People in a harbour café later remembered something more serious. McLellan, they said, had promised to get the captain before the ship reached Norfolk.
Wormell kept him on anyway. On the 9th of January, 1921, the Deering sailed for Hampton Roads, Virginia, a trip of about three weeks.
Late that month she came up to the Cape Lookout lightship, a floating lighthouse anchored off the North Carolina coast. The keeper, Captain Jacobson, watched her come close.
A tall, thin man with reddish hair and a foreign accent called across through a megaphone. The ship had lost her anchors in a storm, he said. Please tell the owners.
Jacobson noticed two things. The man did not look or act like an officer. And the crew were milling around on the quarterdeck, a part of the ship ordinary sailors were not normally allowed.
Someone on the lightship also took a photograph, the last known picture of the Carroll A. Deering under sail. Jacobson's radio was out, so the message never reached the company.
A few days later, the lookout at Cape Hatteras saw her stranded on the outer shoals, sails set, with nobody moving on deck.
Captain James Carlson of the wrecking tug Rescue boarded on the 4th of February. The wheel was smashed, the binnacle broken in, and the rudder loose from its stock.
Salvage crews stripped what they could. The rest of the hull was declared a danger to shipping and blown apart with explosives in March 1921.
In April, a Buxton fisherman named Christopher Columbus Gray reported finding a bottle in the surf with a note inside.
It read, in part, Deering captured by oil burning boat something like chaser. Handcuffing crew. The Wormell family believed the handwriting was the engineer's.
That spring, the captain's daughter, Lula Wormell, refused to let the case fade. With her pastor and Captain Merritt, she took it to Washington.
It reached Herbert Hoover, then Secretary of Commerce. His department ran the nation's lighthouses, and he was worried by other ships that had vanished along the same stretch of ocean.
One was the Hewitt, a sulphur freighter that disappeared at about the same time. Commerce, Treasury, Justice, the Navy and the State Department all opened files on the Deering.

Handwriting experts disagreed about the note. Under questioning by Hoover's investigator, Lawrence Richey, Gray admitted he had written it himself. He had reportedly hoped the attention would win him a job at the Hatteras light.
With the note exposed as a fake, investigators were left with the ship itself, and the ship told a story that did not quite add up.
The men had taken the log, the papers, the chronometer and the navigating instruments. They had also taken their good clothing. Whoever left had time to choose.
Yet signal flags, stores and a great deal of gear were still aboard. The two main anchors were gone, which matched what the man at the lightship had shouted.
The charts were found in the captain's bathroom. That small detail started a rumour along the coast that Wormell had died at sea and been buried before the ship ran aground.
And the food in the galley suggested the crew left not long before a meal, as if something had happened suddenly on an ordinary day.
One of the cats, a grey six-toed tom, was taken ashore. Hatteras historian Danny Couch believes its descendants still live on the Outer Banks.
The National Weather Bureau suggested a storm. But the Deering had been sailing away from the worst weather, and later writers argued that the orderly state of the ship did not look like panic.

The Wormell family was sure it was piracy. A U.S. Shipping Board captain agreed. Investigators even followed rumours that Soviet sympathisers planned to seize American ships. No suspect or evidence was ever found.
Prohibition had begun the year before. Some suggested rum runners took the schooner for smuggling, but no cargo, buyer or witness ever tied her to the trade.
Mutiny had the most support. There was the mate's threat in Barbados, the captain's low opinion of his men, and Jacobson's report of a stranger doing the talking.
Richey and Hoover concluded mutiny was the most likely answer. When a federal agent asked Hatteras Coast Guardsmen whether mutineers could have rowed ashore, their answer was one word: impossible.

Decades later, writers added the Bermuda Triangle to the story, though Diamond Shoals lies north of the area usually drawn on the map. The government's own investigation closed in 1922 without an official finding.
What we know is narrow. Somewhere between Cape Lookout and Diamond Shoals, perhaps over two or three days, eleven men left a ship that was still sailing and took the instruments with them.
The evidence fits a planned departure better than a sudden disaster. Who planned it, and whether Captain Wormell was alive to see it, cannot be proven.
A bow section drifted ashore on Ocracoke Island. Timbers from the hull ended up in houses on Hatteras. In 1955, Hurricane Ione moved the remains again.
Her bell and capstan were later put on display at the Graveyard of the Atlantic Museum in Hatteras, a few miles from the shoals that held her.
The salvors sent Captain Wormell's Bible home to his daughter in Maine. Lula Wormell had carried the case all the way to Washington. She never got an answer.

The best record of the Deering's last week is still that photograph from the lightship: a ship under sail, and a crew who would be gone within days, leaving three cats, the lights still burning, and supper on the stove.
